questions.q: The following sentence has been split into segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error. If you don’t find any error, mark ‘No error’ as your answer.
o: he missed the college bus
unpardonably lately in the morning
because he woke up
questions.s:
Answer:unpardonably lately in the morning

Explanation:
The error lies in the phrase "unpardonably lately".
The word "lately" means recently (हाल ही में), which does not fit the context of waking up late on a specific morning.

The correct word should be "late", and the correct adverb form for how he woke up is "unpardonably late" – अक्षम्य रूप से देर से.

Let’s correct the sentence:
He missed the college bus because he woke up unpardonably late in the morning.

So, the error is in the segment "unpardonably lately in the morning".

questions.q: He was so excitedly as he was nervous before the performance.
o: He was so excitedly as
questions.s:
A positive degree of adjective/adverb comes in between ‘as……as’ and ‘so……as’. So, the correct choice is: (d) He was so excitedly as

The corrected sentence would be: “He was so excited as he was nervous before the performance.”

questions.q: This book is informative than entertaining.
questions.s:

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate form of comparative degree that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.

Bilingual children are so intelligent than those who speak just one language.
questions.s:
The underlined phrase "so intelligent than" is incorrect for a comparative structure. "More intelligent than" correctly uses "more" for the comparative degree of "intelligent" and "than" for comparison.

"So intelligent to"-Incorrect because "so" is not used with "to" in comparisons; it requires "that" in different structures.

"Better intelligent than"-Incorrect because "better" is the comparative form of "good," not "intelligent." The correct form is "more intelligent."

"The most intelligent to"-Incorrect because "the most" is superlative, not comparative, and "to" is not used in comparisons.

Hence, the correct answer is option (c).

Note:

· The Positive Degree is used to denote the mere existence of some quality of what we speak about. It is used when no comparison is made.

· The Comparative degree denotes a higher degree of quality than the positive and is used when two things are compared.

· The Superlative degree indicates the highest degree of quality and is used when more than two things (or sets of things) are compared.
